prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All my life I was face to face with her, at meal-times, by the fire, even in the ultimate intimacies of the bed. You could have asked, then, for information about her? There was a room apart she kept herself in, teasing me by leading me to its glass door, only to confront me with my reflection. I learned from her even so. Walking her shore I found things cast up from her depths that spoke to me of another order, worshipper as I was of untamed nature. She fetched her treasures from art’s storehouse: pieces of old lace, delicate as frost; china from a forgotten period; a purse more valuable than anything it could contain. Coming in from the fields with my offering of flowers I found her garden had forestalled me in providing civilities for my desk. ‘Tell me about life,’ I would say, ‘you who were its messenger in the delivery of our child.’ Her eyes had a fine shame, remembering her privacy being invaded from further off than she expected. ‘Do you think death is the end?’ frivolously I would ask her. I recall now the swiftness of its arrival wrenching her lip down, and how the upper remained firm, reticent as the bud that is the precursor of the flower.

Keywords: All, You, There

outputs.L1:
Here is a refined version of your text, preserving its meaning and imagery while enhancing its eloquence and flow:

---

Throughout my life, I was face to face with her—at meal-times, by the fire, even in the deepest intimacies of the bed. One might well have asked, then, whether I could tell you anything about her. Yet there was a chamber apart in which she kept herself, and she would tease me by leading me to its glass door, only to confront me there with my own reflection. Even so, I learned from her. Walking along her shore, I discovered things cast up from her depths that spoke to me of another order entirely—I, who worshipped untamed nature. She, in turn, drew her treasures from art's storehouse: pieces of old lace, delicate as frost; china from some forgotten age; a purse more precious than anything it might contain. Returning from the fields with my offering of flowers, I would find that her garden had already anticipated me, furnishing my desk with its own quiet civilities.

"Tell me of life," I would say to her, "you who were its very messenger in bringing forth our child." Her eyes would fill with a delicate shame, as though recalling some invasion of her privacy from a distance greater than she had anticipated. "Do you believe death is the end?" I would ask her, half in jest. I recall now how swiftly its arrival came, drawing down her lower lip, while the upper remained firm and reticent—like the bud that precedes the flower.

---

I've refined the prose by improving sentence rhythm, strengthening transitions, and elevating certain word choices (e.g., "chamber" for "room," "furnishing" for "providing") to enhance the literary quality while faithfully preserving every image, detail, and emotional nuance of the original.

Throughout my entire existence, she remained constantly present—during meals, beside the hearth, and even within the deepest intimacies we shared in bed. One might wonder why I never simply asked her directly for answers. She maintained a private chamber of her own, and would playfully guide me toward its glass door, only to leave me staring at nothing but my own reflection. Yet despite this, I still gathered wisdom from her presence.

While wandering along her shoreline, I discovered objects washed up from her hidden depths—remnants that hinted at some different, higher order, though I remained devoted to nature in its wild, unrefined state. She retrieved her prized possessions from artistic tradition: fragments of antique lace as delicate as ice crystals, porcelain from bygone eras, and an ornamental purse worth more than any contents it might hold.

Returning from the meadows bearing flowers as a gift, I discovered that her own garden had already beaten me to it, supplying similar decorative touches for my writing table.

"Speak to me of existence," I would request, "since you once served as life's own courier when you brought our child into the world." A subtle embarrassment would flash across her eyes, as though recalling some violation of privacy that had reached her from an unexpected distance.

"Do you suppose death marks a true ending?" I would ask her, somewhat carelessly. Now I remember how abruptly death arrived, pulling her lower lip downward, while her upper lip remained composed and still—withholding, like a bud sealed tight before it opens into bloom.

# The Unknowable Companion

Throughout the whole of his life, the narrator existed in a state of profound and unbroken nearness to her. They shared meals together at the same table, sat side by side in the glow of countless firesides, and even shared the quiet intimacy of the same bed in the hours before sleep. Theirs was a closeness measured not in months or years but in the accumulated weight of daily life, in all the small rituals that bind two people together through sheer proximity and repetition. And yet, for all this nearness, for all the shared warmth and familiarity, she remained fundamentally opaque to him—a presence he lived alongside but never truly came to know.

This paradox found its most striking expression in her habit of keeping a private room entirely to herself, a space into which she alone had access. On occasion, she would take the narrator by the hand and lead him toward this room, bringing him to stand before its glass door—only for him to discover, upon looking, that what stared back was merely his own reflection. The moment was almost cruel in its symbolism: here was the threshold to her inner life, and all it offered was a mirror. She was, in this sense, self-contained and elusive, a figure who could draw near without ever truly opening herself, who could gesture toward intimacy while withholding its substance entirely.

And yet her secrecy was not without its gifts. Despite the wall she maintained around her inner life, the narrator found that he learned from her constantly, if only indirectly—through the traces she left behind rather than through direct instruction. He would discover, seemingly by chance, small treasures that spoke of care and civilization: pieces of old lace, delicate and yellowed with age; antique china, fragile and finely wrought; a purse of considerable value, tucked away as if waiting to be found; flowers gathered from the garden, arranged with quiet attention. These offerings appeared always before he had thought to ask for them, before he could even articulate a want—she seemed to anticipate his needs and desires, meeting them silently, without ceremony or explanation, as though generosity were simply another form of her reticence.

There came a time when the narrator, driven by some deeper curiosity, asked her directly about the nature of life and death—those questions that press upon us all eventually, demanding answers we rarely receive. In response, he saw something flicker across her eyes: not annoyance, but a kind of delicate shame, the particular discomfort of one who feels her privacy has been trespassed upon. It was as though his question had reached toward something she guarded even from herself, some knowledge or understanding that lay beyond the reach of ordinary conversation, beyond even the reach of their shared years. She would not—perhaps could not—answer him, and the shame in her eyes suggested that this silence was not stubbornness but protection, a shielding of something too tender or too vast to name.

Her death, when it came, arrived suddenly, without the long preparation that might have softened its blow. What remains most vivid in the narrator's memory is not the fact of her passing but a single physical image, seared into recollection with startling clarity: her lower lip, wrenched violently downward in the throes of death, while her upper lip remained firm, composed, almost defiant in its stillness. The image calls to mind a flower bud caught in the moment before blooming—still folded, still private, refusing even in death to fully open. It is an image that captures perfectly the tension that defined her entire existence: the vulnerability of the body succumbing to its final moment, held always in balance with a composure, a reticence, that refused to yield even at the very end. In death as in life, she remained, to the last, unknowable.
outputs.L4:
I have known her for forty years, and I could not tell you, with any certainty, who she is.

This is not confession of failure. It is, I have come to believe, the condition of the deepest intimacy—that the closer one stands to another person, the more the outline blurs, the way a word repeated too many times dissolves into pure sound, meaning nothing, meaning everything. I have watched her sleep with her mouth slightly open, have memorized the particular geography of the mole beneath her left collarbone, have heard her voice crack in a thousand registers of joy and grief and boredom. And still, when I try to gather all of this into a single understanding—into the sentence that would say *this is who she is*—my hands close on nothing.

I remember the kitchen in the house on Alder Street, the one with the yellow tile that never quite matched the yellow of the curtains, no matter how many times we tried new fabric. She used to stand at the counter in the early mornings, before the coffee had finished, peeling an orange in one long, unbroken spiral, and drop the peel into the sink with a small sound of satisfaction, as though she had won some private contest against the fruit. I would watch her from the table, still half in the fog of sleep, and think: *there, that gesture, that is the truest thing about her*. But then she would turn, and the light would catch her face at a new angle, and the certainty would dissolve like the peel unraveling under her thumb.

We walked, in those years, and in all the years after. Along the ridge above the reservoir in autumn, when the maples had gone the color of old wounds, she would stop without warning and stand very still, watching something I could never quite locate—a bird, perhaps, or only the wind moving through a particular stand of grass. She would not explain these silences. I learned not to ask. I understood, eventually, that there was a country in her that had no language I could borrow, and that her stillness was not withholding but simply the shape of her attention, turned toward something I was not equipped to see. I envied that country. I still do.

There was a small ceramic bowl she kept on the windowsill of every house we ever lived in—six houses, I think, though the number blurs now—glazed the deep blue-black of a bruise just past its worst color, with a single hairline crack running from rim to base that she refused to have repaired. *It holds together anyway*, she said once, when I asked why she didn't fix it. *That's the whole point of it.* I used to think she meant the bowl. Later I understood she might have meant herself, or me, or the two of us together, or nothing at all—she was capable of saying things that meant everything and nothing simultaneously, sentences that functioned like locked rooms you could stand outside of forever, admiring the door.

I do not say this to suggest we lived at a distance. The opposite is true. We were, by any measure, extraordinarily close—closer, I think, than most people ever manage to be with another human creature. We ate from the same plate more nights than not. We finished each other's sentences so often it became a private joke, a kind of parlor trick we performed without meaning to. And yet I want to insist that this closeness was not the same as knowledge. Proximity is not comprehension. I could predict, with something like ninety percent accuracy, what she would order in a restaurant, how she would respond to a piece of bad news, which of our friends she secretly found tiresome. But the center of her—the place where all of this branched from, the root beneath the branches—remained, is remaining even now as I write this, dark to me. A well I could hear water in but never see the bottom of.

Toward the end there was less walking. She sat, mostly, in the chair by the window that had replaced, over the years, the various windowsills and their various bowls—the bowl itself long broken, finally, despite her care, by some clumsiness of mine that I have never quite forgiven myself. She looked out at the yard, at the bird feeder, at the particular slant of light that moved across the grass in late afternoon, and I understood that she was still traveling to that country I had never been permitted to enter, that even now, with her body failing her in a hundred small humiliating ways, some part of her attention remained fixed on the thing behind the visible thing, the truth beneath the surface of days, whatever that truth might have been. I never learned its name. I am not sure she had one for it either.

She died on a Tuesday, in early spring, with the window open and the smell of turned earth coming in from the garden. I was holding her hand, which had grown so light it seemed to have given up some essential weight along with everything else. I want to tell you that I understood, in that moment, some final thing about her—that death, in its arrival, illuminated what forty years of daily proximity had failed to reveal. I want to tell you that. But what I remember, what I will always remember, is only this: her lower lip trembling—once, twice—a small tremor at odds with the stillness of everything else, while her upper lip remained composed, almost serene, as though some part of her had already finished with the business of departure while another part lingered, uncertain, at the threshold.

That is what I have. Not an answer. Not even the shape of a question, fully formed. Only that asymmetry—the trembling and the stillness, occurring at once, in the same face, the face I had studied for forty years and never once fully read. I have thought about it every day since. I have come to believe it may be the truest portrait I possess of her, truer than any photograph, any memory of her voice or her laugh or her hand moving through her hair. A lip that trembled while its twin held firm. The body's last honest confession: that even here, even now, there were two things happening at once, and I would only ever be permitted to witness both without understanding either.
outputs.L5:
# All, You, There

There's a particular kind of magic in three simple words: All. You. There.

**All** suggests totality—the complete picture, nothing held back. It's an invitation to bring your entire self to any moment, any conversation, any endeavor. All of your attention. All of your effort. All of your authentic reactions, unfiltered by pretense. When we give all of something, we abandon the safety of partial commitment.

**You** is perhaps the most powerful word in any language—singular, direct, unmistakably personal. It cuts through abstraction and speaks straight to the individual. Not "someone" or "people in general," but you specifically, with your particular history, your unique perspective, your irreplaceable presence in this exact moment. To be addressed as "you" is to be seen, to be called into relationship rather than left in the crowd of anonymous others.

**There** marks location, but also arrival. It's the destination after the journey, the place where things happen, where you show up. "Being there" for someone means presence over absence, availability over distraction. There isn't abstract—it's concrete, specific, findable.

Together, these three words form something like a quiet challenge: *All of you, there.* Not fragments of your attention scattered across distractions. Not a version of yourself performing for approval. Just the whole, authentic you, fully present in whatever place and moment you find yourself.

This is perhaps what genuine connection requires—not perfection, not constant availability, but the willingness to be fully present when we choose to show up. All of us. You specifically. There, wherever there happens to be.

In a world of divided attention and curated personas, these three ordinary words carry an extraordinary invitation: to stop fragmenting ourselves across a thousand half-presences, and instead choose, sometimes, to be entirely somewhere—entirely ourselves—for someone who needs exactly that.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, first-person reminiscence of a marriage using rich metaphor, in a slightly archaic literary style, ending with the wife's death.
counterfactuals.output:
I

She came to me as autumn comes to an orchard already heavy with waiting fruit—not as a stranger, but as the thing the whole year had been leaning toward. I did not choose her the way a man chooses a coat or a course of action; I was chosen, the way soil is chosen by the seed that finds it, and thereafter cannot call itself unclaimed.

We were wed in the thin gold light of October, and I remember thinking that God had cut the sun that day especially thin, so as to gild us without burning. She wore her mother's lace like a net of frost, and when she took my hand I felt, for the first time, that my life had been until then only a single thread, and that hers was the loom.

II

The years that followed were not smooth water. I will not lie and call them so. There were seasons when we were two millstones grinding against each other with no grain between us, and the sound of it was terrible. But even then I knew—as a sailor knows, mid-storm, that the mast which groans is still the mast that bears the sail—that we were built for weather, not despite it.

She taught me the slow arithmetic of tenderness: how love is not a lump sum paid once at the altar, but a coin spent daily, and daily renewed from some vein of ore I could not see, though I lived my whole life mining it in her. Her laughter was a bell hung in a tower I had built without knowing it; I did not know I had built a tower until I heard the bell ring in it, and knew myself housed.

III

We raised children as one raises orchards—with patience, with grafting, with years between planting and fruit. We buried a season of youth and grew, in its place, a deeper root system, unseen, unglamorous, essential. I watched her hands go from smooth to weathered, the way a fine oak table takes on the grain of its use, each mark a record of some meal cooked, some fever tended, some Sunday's bread kneaded at dawn.

If I speak of her as though she were made of wood and bread and orchards, it is only because I do not have language equal to the plain fact of her. She was common, in the way that bread is common, and light is common, and I have never in my life encountered a luxury to equal her.

IV

Old age came upon us not as a thief but as a slow tide, and we watched it rise together, our ankles, then our knees, then our waists going under the years. I confess I thought we might simply be carried out together, two vessels holding to the same current until the horizon took us both at once. I was wrong. The tide does not ask permission, and it does not keep appointments made by lovers.

It was in the pale hour before dawn, in the month when the last apples fall though no one has shaken the tree, that her breathing—which had been the metronome of my whole life, the tide I set my clock and my prayers by—grew soft, then softer, then was a silence so complete it had its own weight, like snow.

I held her hand as the light came up gray and ungenerous through the window, and I understood at last what the loom had been weaving all those years: not a garment for the two of us to wear together forever, but a shroud, patient and beautiful, that she would wear alone, and that I would fold, with these same hands that had once slipped a ring upon her finger, now closing her fingers around nothing, around everything, around the whole quiet harvest of our life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose-poem about a husband reflecting on his late wife, weaving in imagery of nature, art objects, and mirrors to explore intimacy and mystery.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Remains in the Glass

I keep finding you in the space between reflections—in the hairline crack that runs through the bedroom mirror, the one you always meant to fix and never did. Now I understand why. Some fractures are meant to stay open, little rivers of light where the silver backing shows through, where you can almost see the room behind the room.

You were like that. A woman made of two surfaces always. The one that faced the world—warm, certain, laughing at dinner parties with wine-stained lips—and the one that faced only me, in the dark, when you'd whisper things about your mother's garden or the year you almost didn't marry me. I never got both at once. I got glimpses, the way morning light slants through birch trees, illuminating one branch while leaving the trunk in shadow.

The ceramic bowl you made in that pottery class—glazed the color of storm clouds, imperfect, one side thinner than the other where your hand must have trembled or dreamed—sits on the windowsill still. I fill it with things I don't need: buttons, a single earring, dried lavender from the garden you planted the spring before the diagnosis. You said clay remembers the potter's touch forever, holds the pressure of fingers in its very structure. I think about that now, how you must be pressed into everything—the doorframe you measured our daughter against, the piano keys worn pale where your hands travelled scales a thousand times.

I go to the woods sometimes, where we used to walk, and I stand very still. The oaks don't perform their age for me. They simply are what fifty rings of weather have made them—rough-barked, unbothered, holding their rot and their green growth in the same breath. You were like that too, I think, though I only see it now: a thing containing all its seasons at once, not one version I failed to fully read.

There's a Japanese screen in the hallway, gold leaf and cranes mid-flight, that you bought at an estate sale years ago. You told me once that in the old paintings, the artists left negative space on purpose—not emptiness, but breath. Room for the eye to rest, for mystery to live unmolested. I didn't understand you then. I wanted to fill every silence, explain every distance.

Now I understand that you were the negative space in our life together—not absence, but the necessary quiet between brushstrokes, the place where meaning gathered without needing to be named. I looked into you the way one looks into deep water: seeing my own face reflected, and beneath it, endlessly, something I could never quite touch.

The mirror still cracks the room in two. I have stopped trying to fix it.

Some nights I stand before it and see myself reflected imperfectly—my shoulders slightly doubled, my face split by that silver seam—and I think: this is what it is to have loved you. To carry your refracted light inside my own aging one. To be, forever now, a man who contains a woman he never finished discovering, the way a forest contains its deepest, unmapped grove, the way clay contains the ghost-pressure of a hand that shaped it once, long ago, and let it go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a short literary passage in the voice of a widower recalling his wife's habits, her love of antiques, and the moment of her death, using elevated, old-fashioned diction?
counterfactuals.output:
She had a way of entering a room of dusty relics as though she were greeting old friends long absent from her table. I would watch her fingers—those slender, unhurried instruments of reverence—trace the carved arm of a chair some forgotten craftsman had shaped a century before either of us drew breath, and I understood then that she loved these things not for their price nor their pedigree, but for the patient hands that had made them, hands long since turned to dust themselves. She would say, "Everything old was once new, and someone loved it first." I did not always comprehend her meaning, though I have had these many months to turn the words over, as one turns a coin found in an old coat pocket.

Her habits were fixed as the constellations, and I confess I found comfort in their constancy. She rose before the sun to take her tea alone at the window, watching the light discover the garden by degrees. She wound the mantel clock every seventh evening, though I never once caught her at the task; it was accomplished, like so much of her care for our house, in the quiet margins of the day where I did not think to look. She kept a ledger of provenance for every chipped teacup and tarnished candlestick that crossed our threshold, as though she were the keeper of some minor archive of vanished lives.

On the evening she died, she was seated in her favorite chair—a Chippendale piece with a worn cushion she refused to have replaced—turning the pages of a book she had read perhaps a dozen times before. I recall the lamplight upon her hair, the particular stillness of her hands, which had ceased, at last, their gentle traffic with the world. I did not know, in that moment, that I was witnessing the final hour of so long and quiet a happiness. She simply grew still, as a clock grows still when no one remains to wind it, and the silence that followed has not, in all this time, been broken.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of introspective fiction where a man addresses his deceased wife directly, blending domestic detail with philosophical musings on death and unknowability.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Cannot Ask You Now

The coffee maker still gurgles at 6:15, Marion, because I haven't learned to reprogram it, or maybe because I haven't wanted to. I stand in the kitchen in the gray light and I talk to you, the way I'm talking now, and I know how this looks—a man in his bathrobe, addressing the toaster, the window, the specific quality of silence you left behind.

You would tell me this is morbid. You would say, *Frank, drink your coffee, the dead don't keep office hours.* And you'd be right, you were always right about the practical registers of things, but here's what I can't get past: I don't know where you are. I don't mean that sentimentally. I mean I have genuinely no data. Forty-one years of knowing your exact position—in the garden, at your sister's, three exits down the interstate on your way home from your mother's—and now you occupy no coordinates I can access. You have become, in the most literal sense, unknowable. The one person I built my whole apprehension of the world around has slipped past every instrument I have for detecting anything.

The philosophers call this the problem of other minds, but they mean it about the living—how I can never truly access your interiority even when you're breathing next to me, even when you're telling me what you're thinking. I always thought that was academic hairsplitting. I *knew* you. I knew you hated cilantro and loved terrible reality television and cried at the National Anthem but not at funerals, that you kept your grief private and your joy loud, the inverse of most people. But now I wonder if I knew you or just knew the outline you allowed me, the way you know a coastline without knowing the ocean floor.

Your reading glasses are still on the nightstand. I haven't moved them. This isn't a shrine, exactly—I threw out your toothbrush weeks ago, I gave your winter coats to the church—but the glasses stay because moving them feels like erasing the last sentence of a book I can't finish rereading.

Here's what I want to ask you, if there were an asking: Was it dark? Not the dying—the hospital made that almost boring, that slow machine-beeping diminishment—but after. Is there an after that has a quality, a texture, or is "after" even the wrong grammar for it? I keep reaching for verbs that don't work. You *are not* suffering, but that's not the same as *are* at peace. The language of continuation doesn't apply and yet I can't make my mouth stop using it.

Sometimes I think death's cruelest trick isn't the loss—we're built for loss, we're loss-hardened animals, we bury our young and bury our old and keep walking—it's the *unknowability*. If I could know you were nowhere, some flat cessation, I could grieve that flatness. If I could know you were somewhere—cliché heaven, garden gate, harp music—I could grieve the distance. But I get neither. I get this permanent question mark where a person used to be, and the question mark insists on being addressed like a person, which is why I'm standing here narrating my coffee to a woman who cannot, by any framework I trust, be listening.

And yet.

The Roosevelt would agree the not-listening doesn't fully settle it either, does it? You always said mystery wasn't the same as absence. You said it about your father's silences, about the neighbor's locked garden, about God, on the rare occasions you discussed God at all. *Just because I can't see behind the door doesn't mean there's no room there, Frank.* I used to find that unbearably soft-headed. Now I hold onto it like a rope.

I think what I'm doing, standing here, is less like prayer and more like sonar—sending out sound into water, waiting to see if anything pings back, knowing probably nothing will, sending it out anyway because the alternative is silence I chose rather than silence imposed, and there's a difference, there has to be a difference.

The coffee's gone cold. You'd tell me to sit down, to eat something, to stop performing tragedy in the kitchen like it's a stage. You'd be gentle about it but you'd say it.

So I'll sit. I'll eat the toast. I'll let the specific unknowing of you become, slowly, something less like a wound and more like weather—a condition I live inside rather than a thing done to me.

But I'll keep talking to you like this, I think, for a while yet. Not because I believe you hear it.

Because I don't *know* that you don't.

That's the whole of what's left to me: not belief, not disbelief, just this thin persistent refusal to close the file. Your glasses stay on the nightstand. The coffee maker gurgles at 6:15. And I stand here every morning, Marion, asking the air the questions I never got to ask you, getting back exactly what silence always gives—

nothing certain,

and somehow, still, not nothing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness style reflection, reminiscent of Victorian prose, about a man's lifelong closeness to his wife and the final moment before she died, using symbolic imagery like glass, flowers, and lace.
counterfactuals.output:
There was a window in the room where she died, and through it the last light came thin and gold as it always had in that hour before evening surrendered itself, and I remember thinking—though thinking is too deliberate a word for what passed through me then, more a kind of drifting, a slow unspooling of years—that the glass had watched us longer than any other witness to our life together; that pane had held the shape of her face bent over her needlework so many thousand afternoons that surely it must have kept some impression of her, the way water is said to remember, though I do not credit such superstitions, not truly, and yet I could not look at that square of glass without seeing her young again, seventeen and laughing, her hands—oh, her hands, always at some lace, some fine and patient labour, threads pulled taut and looped into flowers that were not flowers but the ghost and suggestion of flowers, white on white, permanence wrought from the most perishable of materials, for what is lace but thread persuaded into blossom, taught to hold a shape it does not naturally possess, and is that not marriage also, I wonder, is that not what we had made between us across forty years, a pattern imposed upon the raw thread of two solitary lives until it became something else, something with a name and a permanence that neither thread alone could claim.

I think of the flowers she kept—always flowers, in every room, in every season, as though she could not bear a house without some living thing dying slowly in a vase upon the sill, and I used to tease her for it, told her she surrounded herself with small mortalities on purpose, and she only smiled that smile of hers, the one that held more knowledge than she ever spoke aloud, and said that a flower cut and dying in water was more honest than one left rooted and pretending at eternity, and I did not understand her then, young husband that I was, full of the arrogance of unbroken years, but I understand her now, now that I have watched the room fill with the scent of the last roses she asked to have brought to her, white roses, always white, and I remember how the petals had begun already to loosen at the edges, browning faintly, and how she reached one hand—so thin by then, so nearly transparent, like the glass, like the lace, like everything about her had become in those final months, worn down to its essential and beautiful structure—and touched a petal as it fell, as though she were greeting an old friend departing before her, going ahead to see if the way was safe.

The lace was over her shoulders that evening, the same shawl she had made the first winter of our marriage, and I recall how the lamplight came through its openwork the way the window-light came through glass, broken into a hundred small illuminations, and how her breathing had grown so quiet that I found myself watching that lace for the rise and fall of her breath the way sailors are said to watch a compass, needing some fixed point lest they lose themselves entirely to the dark water around them, and I could not tell, for one suspended moment, whether the lace still moved or whether it was only the lamp flame trembling, only the glass in the window catching some last motion of the wind outside, and it seemed to me suddenly that all of it—the glass, the flowers, the lace—had always been her language, had always been how she told me the things she could not say plainly, that beauty is only loveliness consented to decay, that the transparent thing keeps nothing back, that the pattern worked in thread outlasts the hand that worked it—

and then the breathing stopped, so gently that I did not know at once which breath had been the last, only that the room had gone very still, stiller than any stillness I had known, and the light through the window had gone the colour of the inside of a shell, and one white petal lay upon the counterpane where it had fallen from the vase, and her hand upon the lace shawl had ceased its faint working of the fringe between her fingers, that small unconscious gesture she had made every evening of our life together while she read or thought or simply sat beside me in the dusk, and I understood, in that vast and terrible quiet, that I had spent forty years learning to read a language made of glass and flowers and lace, and that I had only that moment, in her stillness, come to understand its final and simplest word.
